Neonates of Heteromys salvini emerge from the womb weighing approximately 1.9 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.9 grams], a remarkably diminutive mass for a rodent that will ultimately attain a substantially larger adult body size. This altricial birth mass reflects a relatively brief intrauterine development period, during which the gestating embryo undergoes rapid organogenesis but deposits limited reserves of subcutaneous fat. Under captive conditions maintained at a core body temperature of 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C], the typical interval between successive parturition events is governed by a modest reproductive rate; field records indicate that females produce approximately 1 to 2 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 to 2 litters per year], with each litter containing an average of 3.8 pups [N_R_i = each litter containing an average of 3.8 pups]. This conservative reproductive output aligns with ecological expectations for a spiny pocket mouse inhabiting seasonal Neotropical forests where resource availability fluctuates markedly across the year. The combination of small litters and infrequent breeding events likely reflects an evolved strategy that prioritizes maternal survival and prolonged investment in each offspring, rather than the high fecundity typical of many muroid rodents.

The intrauterine phase of development in Heteromys salvini proceeds rapidly, with embryo growth and differentiation occurring over a tightly constrained period. Data obtained from laboratory breeding colonies indicate that gestation lasts 27.5 days [tg = 27.5 days] when the female is maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a thermal condition that approximates the core temperature of a euthermic adult. This gestational interval, falling within the range of 27 to 28 days reported across multiple studies, is characteristic of heteromyid rodents and reflects the accelerated foetal development typical of this lineage. Upon delivery, the altricial neonate is completely dependent on maternal milk for nourishment, and the suckling juvenile phase is characterized by rapid somatic growth as the newborn pup transitions from endogenous yolk reserves to a diet of lipid-rich milk. The energetic demands of lactation place considerable physiological strain on the female, who must sustain both her own basal maintenance requirements and the nutritional needs of a rapidly growing litter. This tight coupling between maternal thermal homeostasis and foetal development underscores the importance of stable thermoregulatory capacity in determining gestation duration in small endotherms.

Weaning represents a critical developmental milestone in the life cycle of Heteromys salvini, marking the transition from complete nutritional dependence on maternal milk to independent foraging on seeds, fruits, and invertebrate prey. Under the standardized thermal conditions of 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C], the time since birth at weaning for this species is 29 days [tx = 29 days], placing the completion of the nursing stage within a window of 28 to 30 days as corroborated by longitudinal captive studies. This relatively short suckling period is typical among spiny pocket mice and reflects the rapid digestive maturation that enables young to process solid food at an early age. By the time weaning occurs, the weaned juvenile has attained a wet weight at weaning of 26 grams [Wwx = 26 grams], representing a substantial increase over the 1.9 gram birth mass and reflecting the efficiency of maternal milk transfer. Following nutritional independence from the lactating female, the sub-adult individual enters a pre-reproductive period during which continued somatic growth and neural development occur before the onset of reproductive capability. This post-weaning phase is energetically demanding, as the young mammal must acquire and process sufficient resources to support both maintenance and growth in a competitive environment.

Puberty in Heteromys salvini, defined as the attainment of functional gametogenesis and the capacity to engage in successful reproductive activity, occurs after an extended period of juvenile growth and development. Research carried out under controlled laboratory conditions at 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C] has demonstrated that the time since birth at puberty is 193 days [tp = 193 days], a relatively late age at reproductive maturity compared to many similarly-sized muroid rodents. This delayed onset of gonadal maturation likely reflects the substantial energetic investment required to achieve the ultimate wet weight of adulthood, which in fully-grown individuals can reach 65 grams [Wwi = 65 grams], though body mass in natural populations typically ranges from 30 to 65 grams across individuals. The delay before first oestrus or testicular descent allows the sub-adult mammal to accumulate sufficient lipid and protein reserves to support the heightened metabolic demands of reproduction, including gestation and subsequent lactation in females. Once sexual maturity is attained, the breeding adult mammal may persist in a reproductively viable state for a substantial portion of the lifespan, though reproductive success is modulated by seasonal factors such as rainfall patterns and seed crop abundance that influence body condition and the initiation of reproductive activity.

The maximum lifespan of Heteromys salvini, a key demographic parameter that shapes population dynamics and life-history evolution, has been documented through both mark-recapture field studies and long-term captive maintenance. Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species (37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C]), the oldest recorded individuals reach an age of 549 days [am = 549 days] from birth to natural death. This maximum recorded longevity of approximately one and a half years is modest relative to the theoretical lifespan predictions for rodents of this body size, suggesting that extrinsic mortality factors such as predation pressure and environmental stochasticity impose strong constraints on survival in the wild. In captivity, where predators are excluded and food availability is consistent, individuals may approach this upper limit more reliably, with senescent decline characterized by progressive deterioration of organ function and loss of body condition. The relatively short lifespan, coupled with the late age at first reproduction and low annual fecundity, defines a slow-paced life-history strategy that contrasts markedly with the rapid life cycles observed in many other small Neotropical rodents.
